meta.report: R7b geography research for the Earth worldgen mod (Europe, Atlantic, Old World maps)
meta.contract: Only sources fetched in this session are cited. Coordinates are decimal degrees (WGS84), lat then lon, copied programmatically from the cited source; approximate or derived values say so in their basis field.

confidence_scale.high: stated directly in a fetched source (or computed from source polygons) and unambiguous
confidence_scale.medium: single source, representative point rather than true centroid or narrowest point, or sources disagree modestly
confidence_scale.low: estimated, internally inconsistent, or location UNVERIFIED

meta.citation_url_note: Every entry has citation_url (string); destroyed_europe.citation_url is a list of its anchor articles. citation_revision pins the exact Wikipedia revision read.
methods: Wikipedia: MediaWiki API (prop=coordinates with coprimary=all, prop=revisions wikitext) on en.wikipedia, plus de, it and es articles
OpenStreetMap: Overpass API for canal centrelines; Nominatim for two Gibraltar capes
RESOLVE Ecoregions 2017 shapefile: areas, centroids, bounding boxes and simplified outlines computed locally

resolve_area_check.excluded: atlantic_forest (biome vs moist-forest subset) and sundarbans (forest vs mangrove plus swamp ecoregions) are not like-for-like

ranges.name: Alps
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: Arc from the Cadibona pass (Alps-Apennines boundary) to the Semmering; the article says the arch runs from Nice to Trieste and Vienna. The south-east branch to Triglav and the Godovič pass is not drawn.

ranges.name: Pyrenees
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: The article runs the range from the Basque Mountains near the Bay of Biscay to Cap de Creus on the Mediterranean; Larrun (La Rhune) is the researcher's chosen western summit. Aneto is the highest point; whether it sits on the main divide is not verified.

ranges.name: Carpathian Mountains
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: Clockwise arc from the Danube at Devín (Bratislava) to the Iron Gates. Gerlachovský štít (highest summit) and the Ceahlău massif are included as landmark summits; whether they lie on the main watershed is not verified.

ranges.name: Greater Caucasus
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: Article: from the Taman Peninsula (Black Sea) to the Absheron Peninsula (Caspian), traditionally split at Mount Elbrus and Mount Kazbek into Western, Central and Eastern Caucasus; both are vertices, but whether each stands on the watershed itself is not verified. Gap of about 210 km between Tebulosmta and Bazardüzü (no fetched summit in between).

ranges.name: Scandinavian Mountains (Scandes)
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: From the Hardangervidda plateau in southern Norway to Halti in the far north. The range is broad (infobox width 320 km); this line is a spine, not a ridge crest in the Alpine sense.

ranges.name: Apennine Mountains
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: From Altare/Cadibona (article: join the Ligurian Alps at Altare) down the peninsula to Aspromonte above the Strait of Messina.

ranges.name: Balkan Mountains (Stara Planina)
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: Article: conventionally begins at Vrashka Chuka and runs about 560 km to the Black Sea (Cape Emine).

ranges.name: Dinaric Alps
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: North-west to south-east along the Adriatic hinterland; Maja Jezercë is the range high point. Maglić (Bosnia) had no coordinate in the fetched data.

ranges.name: Ural Mountains
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: Article: about 2,500 km from the Kara Sea to the Kazakh steppe, in units from north to south Pay-Khoy, Zapolyarnyy, Pripolyarnyy, Polyarnyy, Severnyy, Sredniy, Yuzhnyy Ural and Mugodzhary; Vaygach Island and Novaya Zemlya continue the chain north. Konstantinov Kamen had no fetched coordinate, so the Pay-Khoy to Payer segment cuts a corner.

ranges.name: Appalachian Mountains

ranges.name: Rocky Mountains
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: Continental Divide spine from Mount Robson to northern New Mexico. Probably outside the Atlantic map. Lower priority.

ranges.name: Andes
ranges.vertex_method: Named summits and passes on or near the main divide, chosen by the researcher and ordered along the range; each vertex coordinate is copied from its linked Wikipedia article. Straight segments between vertices are an approximation of the crest.
ranges.notes: From Pico Bolívar in Venezuela to Fitz Roy in Patagonia (infobox length 8,900 km). Illimani and Sajama make a zigzag where the range runs as parallel cordilleras (not verified in fetched text). Lower priority.

passes.name: Brenner Pass
passes.why_historic: One of the most important transit routes between northern and southern Europe (motorway and railway, Innsbruck to Bolzano); Roman roads over it appear on the Tabula Peutingeriana.

passes.name: Gotthard Pass
passes.why_historic: Vital north-south trade route since the Middle Ages; the region north of it became the nucleus of the Swiss Confederacy in the 13th century; three record-length tunnels.

passes.name: Simplon Pass
passes.why_historic: Gained international significance with Napoleon's Simplon Road (1801 to 1805), built to move artillery between the Rhone valley and Italy.

passes.name: Great St Bernard Pass
passes.why_historic: Used since the Bronze Age with Roman road traces; Napoleon's army crossed into Italy here in 1800; lowest pass on the ridge between Mont Blanc and Monte Rosa.

passes.name: Mont Cenis (Col du Mont-Cenis)
passes.why_historic: Divides the Cottian and Graian Alps; crossed by the Vaudois in 1689 and held by some authors to be Hannibal's pass.
passes.notes: Coordinate is the Mont Cenis article coordinate (massif and pass share an article).

passes.name: Little St Bernard Pass
passes.why_historic: On the main Alpine watershed between Savoie and the Aosta Valley; a prehistoric stone circle lies on the pass, with World War II fortifications.

passes.name: Col de Montgenèvre
passes.why_historic: Known to the Romans before 118 BC, when Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus began road building; one of the principal crossings of the main range between France and Italy; Napoleon obelisk of 1804.

passes.name: Col de Tende
passes.why_historic: Road said (historian Guizot) to have been opened by Phoenicians and kept up by Greeks and Romans; its 1882 road tunnel is among the oldest long road tunnels.

passes.name: Reschen Pass
passes.why_historic: A bridle path linked the Inn and Adige valleys even before the Roman era; crosses the main chain of the Alps.

passes.name: Splügen Pass
passes.why_historic: In use in the Roman era; possibly the Cunus Aureus of the Tabula Peutingeriana.

passes.name: Semmering Pass
passes.why_historic: With the Wechsel Pass, the most important link between Lower Austria and Styria; carries the Semmering Railway.

passes.name: Colle di Cadibona (Bocchetta di Altare)
passes.why_historic: Traditional boundary between the Alps and the Apennines, between Savona and Altare.

passes.name: Somport
passes.why_historic: Latin Summus portus; one of the most popular routes for soldiers, merchants and pilgrims to Santiago on the route from Arles.

passes.name: Roncevaux Pass (Roncesvalles)
passes.why_historic: Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778 (Roland and Charlemagne's rearguard); a customary point on the Santiago de Compostela pilgrimage route.

passes.name: Col du Perthus (Le Perthus)
passes.why_historic: Hannibal's army and elephants crossed in 218 BC; the Roman Summum Pyrenaeum, junction of the Via Domitia and the Via Augusta.
passes.notes: Lowest of the listed Pyrenean crossings.

passes.name: Col de Puymorens
passes.why_historic: Historically crossed the France-Catalonia border until the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees; well travelled since the 18th century.

passes.name: Dukla Pass
passes.why_historic: Lowest pass of the Carpathian main range; strategically significant; bitter battles on the Eastern Fronts of both World Wars.

passes.name: Verecke Pass (Veretskyi Pass)
passes.why_historic: Hungarian tribes entered the Carpathian Basin through it in 895; well travelled for more than a millennium.

passes.name: Uzhok Pass
passes.why_historic: On the San and Uzh watershed near the Poland-Ukraine border; scene of fierce fighting in World War I.

passes.name: Tihuța Pass (Borgo Pass)
passes.why_historic: Links Bistrița (Transylvania) with Vatra Dornei (Bukovina); the 'Borgo Pass' of Bram Stoker's Dracula.

passes.name: Turnu Roșu Pass (Red Tower Pass)
passes.why_historic: The Olt river's passage through the Southern Carpathians, linking Transylvania (Sibiu) and Wallachia (Vâlcea).
passes.notes: River gorge pass; very low (352 m).

passes.name: Predeal Pass
passes.why_historic: Separates the Southern from the Eastern Carpathians; the main route between Bucharest and Brașov.

passes.name: Iron Gates (Danube gorge)
passes.why_historic: Danube gorge on the Serbia-Romania border, 134 km in the broad sense; the river route through the Carpathian-Balkan barrier.
passes.notes: A river passage, not a road pass.

passes.name: Darial Gorge
passes.why_historic: Terek gorge at the east foot of Kazbek; fortified in antiquity as the Iberian or Caucasian Gates (Strabo's Porta Caucasica); carries the Georgian Military Road.

passes.name: Jvari Pass (Georgian Military Road)
passes.elevation_basis: Georgian Military Road text: maximum altitude 2,379 m at the Jvari Pass, coordinate 42.5042 N 44.4538 E
passes.why_historic: Highest point of the Georgian Military Road, the historic route across the Caucasus from Georgia to Russia.
passes.notes: Coordinate is the article's inline coordinate for the pass.

passes.name: Mamison Pass
passes.why_historic: On the central Greater Caucasus crest; crossed by the Ossetian Military Road (Kutaisi to Alagir).

passes.name: Derbent coastal gateway
passes.why_historic: Occupies the narrow gateway between the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus, linking the Eurasian steppe to the south; the coastal way around the range.
passes.notes: City coordinate; not a mountain pass.

passes.name: Filefjell (Kongevegen)
passes.elevation_basis: infobox 1,920 m is the massif, not the road summit; road summit elevation not in fetched text
passes.why_historic: The historical and modern main route between Western and Eastern Norway; the old trail is the Filefjell Kongevegen (King's Road).
passes.notes: Coordinate is the area article coordinate.

passes.name: Hjerkinn (Dovrefjell crossing)
passes.elevation_basis: Hjerkinn Station on the Dovre Line at 1,017 m (village infobox 990 m)
passes.why_historic: Where the Dovre Line railway and the E6 cross the Dovrefjell plateau.
passes.notes: Historic role (pilgrim and royal road over Dovrefjell) not verified in fetched text.

passes.name: Cisa Pass
passes.why_historic: Divides the Ligurian and Tuscan Apennines between Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna, near the source of the Magra.
passes.notes: Text gives 1,040 m, infobox 1,041 m. Via Francigena link not verified in fetched text.

passes.name: Futa Pass
passes.elevation_basis: lead text 'at an elevation of 903 m'
passes.why_historic: On the Florence-Bologna road; part of the Gothic Line in World War II, with a German military cemetery nearby.

passes.name: Shipka Pass
passes.why_historic: Scene of a series of battles in the 1877 to 1878 war (Battle of Shipka Pass); links Gabrovo and Kazanlak.
passes.notes: Infobox 1,190 m, lead text 1,150 m (sources disagree).

passes.name: Petrohan Pass
passes.why_historic: Shortest route between Sofia and north-western Bulgaria; part of Pan-European Corridor IV.

passes.name: Beklemeto (Troyan) Pass
passes.why_historic: Main road between Troyan and the Karlovo plain in north-central Bulgaria.

passes.name: Kotel Pass
passes.why_historic: On one of the main routes connecting northern and southern Bulgaria.

passes.name: Iskar Gorge
passes.why_historic: The chief pass through the Balkan Mountains; road and railway from Sofia toward Mezdra.

passes.name: Postojna Gate
passes.why_historic: Section of the Amber Road (Baltic to Adriatic); the Romans fortified it against invasions into Italy (Aquileia to Emona road).

passes.name: Babinov Road (Ural crossing)
passes.why_historic: Found by Artemy Babinov in 1597 and cut through the forest a few years later; for a long time the shortest path across the Urals, Solikamsk to Verkhoturye and on to Tobolsk.
passes.notes: No coordinate for the crest crossing; the point given is the western terminus Solikamsk (eastern terminus Verkhoturye in route_endpoints).

passes.name: Tizi n'Tichka
passes.why_historic: Main High Atlas road from Marrakesh to Ouarzazate, a gateway to the Sahara.
passes.notes: Infobox 2,205 m from a 2022 GPS survey; the summit sign says 2,260 m.

passes.name: Persian Gates (Tang-e Meyran)
passes.why_historic: Battle of the Persian Gate, 330 BC: Alexander the Great against the last Achaemenid resistance; controls the link between the coast and central Persia.

passes.name: Khyber Pass
passes.why_historic: Part of the ancient Silk Road; a vital trade route between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent and a strategic choke point used by many invasions.
passes.notes: Strictly in the Spin Ghar (White Mountains) south of the Hindu Kush proper.

passes.name: Salang Pass
passes.why_historic: The primary economic and logistical lifeline between northern Afghanistan and the rest of the country.

passes.name: Khawak Pass
passes.why_historic: Route traditionally thought to have been followed by Alexander the Great across the Hindu Kush from the Panjshir valley.

passes.name: Wakhjir Pass
passes.why_historic: The only potentially navigable pass between Afghanistan and China, at the east end of the Wakhan Corridor.

passes.name: Bolan Pass
passes.why_historic: Natural gateway through the Toba Kakar range in Balochistan.
passes.notes: Not in the Hindu Kush proper; included as the southern companion of the Khyber.

passes.name: Nathu La
passes.why_historic: Described by J. W. Edgar in 1873 as used for trade by Tibetans; used by Younghusband in 1903 to 1904; Sikkim to the Chumbi Valley.

passes.name: Zoji La
passes.why_historic: Connects the Kashmir Valley with the Dras and Suru valleys (Ladakh).

passes.name: Cumberland Gap
passes.why_historic: Famous in American colonial history; frontiersmen led by Daniel Boone opened it to pioneers heading west into Kentucky.

passes.name: Delaware Water Gap
passes.why_historic: Where the Delaware River cuts through a large Appalachian ridge.
passes.notes: Geographic gap; historic role not stated in fetched text.

passes.name: South Pass
passes.why_historic: Continental Divide crossing used by the Oregon, California and Mormon Trails.

passes.name: Lemhi Pass
passes.why_historic: Meriwether Lewis and three members of the Lewis and Clark Expedition crossed the Continental Divide here on 12 August 1805.

passes.name: Kicking Horse Pass
passes.why_historic: Carries the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Trans-Canada Highway across the Continental Divide.

passes.name: Yellowhead Pass
passes.why_historic: Continental Divide crossing between Jasper and Mount Robson parks, traversed by the Canadian National railway (article image caption).

passes.name: Marias Pass
passes.why_historic: Traversed by US Highway 2 and the BNSF Hi-Line; the article calls it the lowest crossing of the Continental Divide (scope of that claim truncated in the extract).

passes.name: Uspallata Pass (Bermejo, Cumbre)
passes.why_historic: Used in 1817 by San Martín's Army of the Andes to free Chile; route between Mendoza and Santiago.

passes.name: Paso Internacional Los Libertadores (Cristo Redentor)
passes.why_historic: Main transport route from Santiago into Mendoza Province.
passes.notes: Modern road crossing next to the Uspallata pass.

destroyed_europe.status: proposal for review (design choice, not a geographic fact)

polygon.anchor: offshore W of the Gironde mouth (Pointe de Grave 45.5694,-1.0639)
Strait of Dover midline: midpoint of South Foreland and Cap Gris-Nez
North Sea offshore NW of Texel
Elbe mouth, set south of Brunsbüttel so the Kiel Canal stays outside
Baltic offshore N of the Pomeranian coast
Vistula Spit at the Poland-Russia border (Vistula Lagoon 54.45,19.75)
Moravian Gate between the Sudetes and the Carpathians (design point, approximate)

rationale: Every edge sits on a feature catalogued in this report, so the zone boundary reads as terrain rather than an arbitrary line.

West and north edges run offshore (Bay of Biscay, Channel, North Sea, Baltic): the whole French, Benelux, German and Polish coast from the Gironde to the Vistula Spit is inside, and the sea is unaffected.
The Channel edge passes through the Strait of Dover midline, so Britain stays outside and the strait stays open water.
The Elbe-to-Baltic edge keeps Schleswig-Holstein north of Brunsbüttel, the Kiel Canal, Denmark, the Belts and the Øresund outside and intact.
The eastern edge follows the Bug line (Terespol, opposite Brest), leaving Białowieża Forest and the Pripet Marshes outside as a natural eastern barrier.
The south-eastern edge follows the northern Carpathian foothills (Przemyśl to the Moravian Gate), so the Carpathian crest and the Dukla, Uzhok and Verecke passes stay outside as entry routes.
The southern edge follows the north foot of the Alps (Lake Neusiedl, Lake Constance, Lake Geneva): every Alpine pass stays outside.

The south-western edge runs from Lake Geneva to the Gironde mouth along the northern rim of the Massif Central, leaving Lyon, Aquitaine, the Landes forest, the Pyrenees and Mediterranean France (Camargue) outside.
destroyed_europe.city_coordinate_source: Wikipedia article coordinates fetched via the MediaWiki GeoData API (see sources); membership computed by ray-casting point-in-polygon in lon/lat

forests_inside: Bohemian Forest (Šumava) with the Bavarian Forest

open_questions: Whether wetlands inside the zone (Wadden Sea, Biebrza) are exempt from destruction.
Whether Vienna, the Swiss Plateau (Basel, Zurich, Bern) and Kraków should be inside; all three currently are.
Whether Kaliningrad Oblast should be inside; it is currently outside.
